Zuni

Zuni’s museum account presents historical learning as community work, including how collections and outside representations are handled. An architectural history and an agency account of Hawikuh provide distinct starting perspectives; the 1873 exterior photograph is a dated outside record, not contemporary community life.

Identity and context

The Pueblo of Zuni is a living nation with its own language, history and institutions.

Read the sources [1] nps.gov

02

A path for deeper reading

Focus the next stage of research on: A:shiwi self-designation, language, land and Zuni-authored histories. The sources below are selected reading paths; their authorship, dates and community scope should guide how they are used.

Read the sources [1] nps.gov [2] New Mexico Legislature (host; authorship unverified) [3] Zuni Pueblo / Visitor Center (New Mexico Legislature-hosted copy)

03

A museum serving its community

The 2021 museum feature dates the institution’s beginnings to 1992 and explains learning and reflection as its purpose. It describes collaboration with collecting institutions to challenge inaccurate representations and improve community access and control. Those stated purposes do not grant visitors access to private knowledge or permission to reproduce collections.

Read the sources [4] Pueblo of Zuni / A:shiwi A:wan Museum and Heritage Center

04

An adapted building and an educational purpose

Burgio-Ericson’s architectural account follows a former trading post’s adaptation into the museum. It relates that reuse to youth learning, archives and collaboration. This selected indexed account offers historical building context; its photographs and underlying records were not inspected.

Read the sources [5] Klinton Burgio-Ericson / Society of Architectural Historians, SAH Archipedia

05

Reading Hawikuh across perspectives

NPS discusses Hawikuh, violent Spanish contact and later colonial conflict. The museum feature presents its own exhibition as a way to learn that history from Zuni perspectives and also questions the legacy of collecting and excavation. Read these accounts together; this guide does not reproduce ceremonial material or infer an unrestricted right to visit.

Read the sources [1] nps.gov [4] Pueblo of Zuni / A:shiwi A:wan Museum and Heritage Center

Hawikuh and Zuni-Cibola Complex — selected agency historical account ↗

NPS follows Hawikuh’s occupation and violent Spanish contact, then later colonial conflict and excavation. It is an outside heritage interpretation to compare with Zuni accounts.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual historical main body, reader lines 42–61, and updated date 25 July 2023. Specific burial, religious-practice and site-access details are not synthesized; linked underlying records uninspected.

Review recorded: October 28, 2026

Access note: Normal public body read. The page contains repeated excavation paragraphs and differing 1917/1918 start wording compared with the museum account; no excavation-start date is asserted. Colonial discovery wording and broad ancestry claims are not adopted.
